quote:
The question is whether a non-negative integer n can be expressed as a^2 + b^2 with a and b non-negative integers.

The submission uses a two-pointer search:

    b = math.isqrt(n)
    while a <= b:
        total = a * a + b * b
        if total < n:
            a += 1
        else:
            b -= 1

a starts at 0 and b at the largest integer whose square does not exceed n, so every candidate pair with a <= b lies between them. When the sum is too small, no pair using the current a with any smaller b can reach n, so a is safely increased; when it is too big, the current b paired with any larger a would only be bigger, so b is decreased. An equality test just before these branches returns True on an exact match. Since the order of a and b does not matter, restricting the search to a <= b loses nothing, and the loop ends with False only after every useful pair has been ruled out.

The visible tests cover 5, 7 and 0. For 13 the search starts at a = 0, b = 3 (sum 9), moves to a = 1 (sum 10), then a = 2 (sum 13) and returns True, matching 4 + 9. For 21 it visits the sums 16, 17, 20, 25 and 18 before a passes b, then returns False, which is right because no two squares add to 21. The case a = b is also allowed, so 2 = 1 + 1 and 8 = 4 + 4 are accepted.

Nothing depends on the particular examples; the search is exhaustive over the relevant range for any n.

Verdict: PASS
paraphrase:
The question is whether a non-negative integer n can be expressed as a^2 + b^2 with a and b non-negative integers.

The submission searches with two indices moving toward each other. The first starts at zero and the second at the integer square root of n, the largest value whose square does not exceed n. On each step it adds the squares of the two indices. If that sum equals n it returns True; if the sum is too small it raises the lower index; if it is too large it lowers the upper index. The loop continues while the lower index does not exceed the upper one and returns False when they cross.

This is a sound search. When the sum is below n, pairing the current lower index with any smaller upper index would give an even smaller sum, so that lower value can be discarded. When the sum is above n, the current upper value paired with any larger lower value would exceed n too, so it can be discarded. Because the order of the two squares does not matter, searching only pairs where the first is at most the second misses nothing.

Besides the visible values 5, 7 and 0, I followed n = 13. The indices start at 0 and 3 with sum 9, then the lower index moves to 1 (sum 10) and 2 (sum 13), and the function returns True, matching 4 plus 9. For 21 the sums visited are 16, 17, 20, 25 and 18 before the indices cross, so it returns False, which is right because no two squares add to 21. Equal indices are allowed, so 2 and 8 are correctly accepted.

No input is singled out, and the search covers every relevant pair for any n.
